region: United Kingdom (North Atlantic, west of Shetland)
key_facts: The UK government granted consent for gas production from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea; the next major decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh concerns the Rosebank field, which is bigger than Jackdaw and would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions. Rosebank's owners are Adura and Ithaca.

Rosebank is operated via a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named Petrojarl Rosebank, chartered from Aberdeen-based Altera, with 122 people on board; the field is located about 80 miles north west of Shetland and contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.

Consent for Rosebank was first granted under the Conservative government in 2023; in 2025 the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals for Rosebank and Jackdaw unlawful for failing to account for the climate impact of burning the extracted fossil fuels. Lord Ericht said work short of producing oil and gas could continue while more detailed environmental assessments were prepared.

Environmental campaigners Greenpeace and Uplift brought the legal challenge; Uplift's executive director Tessa Khan called Rosebank 'a disastrous decision' and urged prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables. Oil from Rosebank would be sold on the international market and most likely taken to continental Europe for refining.
importance_reason: Pending government decision on a large UK oil field with a court-ordered reassessment and a major policy dispute on energy and climate, though no direct market-moving price shock is reported.
market_link: Approval would add a sizeable new UK North Sea oil supply and affect investor sentiment toward UK energy policy and North Sea production outlook; the source does not quantify a price effect.

key_facts: UK government's fiscal 'headroom' (cash buffer for its fiscal rules) may have fallen from around £24bn to as low as £11bn in the last six months, partly due to higher interest rates on government borrowing; the Chancellor may need to raise money to restore it.
Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to raise income tax, VAT or National Insurance rates; capital gains tax increases and extending the mansion tax were reportedly ruled out by government sources.

Tax Policy Associates estimates raising the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 5.5% could raise an additional £1bn–£2bn a year; SMF estimates doubling gaming machine tax from 20% to 40% could raise £275m–£460m; reports suggest making online marketplaces collect VAT could raise around £1bn a year, while the Treasury estimates a £12bn annual 'VAT tax gap'.

The three tax measures combined would raise a maximum of around £3.5bn a year; the Conservatives claim £36bn a year in welfare savings and Reform claim £50bn, which independent analysts question as realistic.

key_facts: Proposition 40 in California would impose a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's roughly 200+ billionaires, aiming to raise about $100bn (£75bn) to offset federal health-care funding cuts linked to Trump's tax and spending bill.

The measure would apply retroactively to those with net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026; at least six billionaires reportedly left the state before that date, and Zuckerberg's possible liability is estimated at up to $12.5bn.

A September poll found 45% of likely voters in favour, 42% opposed and 13% undecided; approval requires a majority of residents. Governor Gavin Newsom and Google co-founder Sergey Brin (over $100m to a political group) oppose it.

The BBC cites European evidence that wealth taxes tend to cause capital flight and raise little revenue (Norway, Switzerland examples); Washington state is separately weighing a 9.9% tax on income above $1m a year.

actors: Florence Eshalomi (министр жилищного строительства и сообществ)
key_facts: The UK government's new statutory Private Parking Code of Practice was laid out in Parliament on Tuesday. It is subject to a 40-day parliamentary scrutiny period and will come into force 21 calendar days after issue.

Maximum parking charge is set at £100, or £60 if paid within a fortnight; operators can still add a £70 debt recovery fee, plus court fees and legal costs. The five-minute payment rule was already banned by the sector's updated code; the five-minute consideration period and 10-minute grace period were already in the sector code.

New elements include cancellation (not just reduction to £20) of charges on appeal for sudden illness, overrunning medical appointments, childcare delays and vehicle breakdown, plus loss of DVLA keeper data access for non-compliant operators. The AA and RAC say the code does not go far enough, as debt recovery fees and an independent single appeals body were not included.
importance_reason: Регуляторное изменение в сфере частной парковки без прямого эффекта на макро- или рынки; значимо для потребителей, но не для финансовых рынков.
